subject: Marginal predictions on probability scale for logistic regression model

messages.author: 8d7e6559e413a92b
messages.subject: Marginal predictions on probability scale for logistic regression model
parts:
Hello, 

I am trying to obtain marginal predictions on the probability scale from a logistic regression model. To do this, I am using the following approach: 


dat <- data.frame(y = rbinom(500, 1, .75))

inla.f <- y ~ 1

m1.inla <- inla(inla.f, family='binomial', data=dat, 
                control.predictor = list(compute=T),
                control.compute = list(waic=T))


n = nrow(dat)
inla.pred = numeric(n)


for(i in 1:n) {
  
  inla.pred[i] = inla.emarginal(
    function(x) psych::logistic(x), 
    m1.inla$marginals.fitted.values[[i]])
}


However, when I do this, I what appear to be wildly inaccurate predictions. 

Oddly, when I don't transform the prediction, I get much more reasonable predictions:  


n = nrow(dat)
inla.pred = numeric(n)


for(i in 1:n) {
  
  inla.pred[i] = inla.emarginal(
    function(x) x, 
    m1.inla$marginals.fitted.values[[i]])
}


For instance, these are much closer to: 

glm.pred <- predict(glm(y~1, data=dat), type='response')

I assume I am just misunderstanding the procedure for estimating marginal predictions in INLA, but it would be great if someone had insight into why the first approach doesn't work and why the second appears to. 

Also, if there is a better approach to do this, I would love to hear about it. 

Thanks!

Best,
Joe

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Marginal predictions on probability scale for logistic regression model
parts:
You could tell inla to produce fitted.values on the natural scale, by setting link=1 (in control.predictor). (The rinla.org FAQ entry is called something like “how do I make predictions with INLA?”)
I don’t have an explanation for why you appear to get reasonable values without applying the link function.

Finn
